summary: This Best Current Practice document describes security measures that can and should be deployed around the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), the protocol almost exclusively used to exchange routing information between networks, since its central role makes its security important.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP is how networks tell each other how to reach places. This guide lists the habits and protections operators should use so no one can easily mess it up.

subtitle: The operator's checklist for keeping BGP sessions, routes and routers from being abused.

tldr.problem: BGP is used almost everywhere to exchange routing information between networks, yet it has no built-in way to check that the routes it carries follow the community's guidelines. Accidents and attacks can disrupt routing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gathers common practices: protect the router and its TCP sessions, filter prefixes, AS paths and next hops, cap the number of prefixes per peer, use route flap dampening with adjusted thresholds, and scrub BGP communities.
tldr.outcome: Operators get a coherent baseline policy for generic Internet peerings, with exceptions allowed where each side agrees. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 194) and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), specified in RFC 4271, is the protocol used to exchange routing information between network domains. BGP itself does not check whether the routes exchanged conform to the guidelines defined by the Internet community. This RFC summarises common existing guidelines and helps network administrators apply coherent BGP policies.

The guidance is meant for generic Internet BGP peerings. Autonomous Systems can agree on exceptions for local needs, which is acceptable, but every exception might affect the entire inter-domain routing environment, so administrators SHOULD weigh the impact first.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP lets networks share directions to each other. It does not check if the directions make sense, so this guide adds sensible checks.

sections.title: Protecting the Speaker and Its Sessions
sections.content:
A BGP speaker SHOULD be protected by an Access Control List that discards packets to TCP port 179 coming from any address that is not a known or permitted neighbor. Without it, a high volume of connection requests can attack the speaker. A control-plane specific ACL (receive-ACL, control-plane policing) is preferred, and rate-limiting accepted BGP traffic MAY be added.

BGP sessions can be attacked, for example with spoofed TCP RST packets, or by injecting packets after ARP spoofing. Protection options are:

  • MD5 protection (RFC 2385), the first mechanism and still the most used because vendors support it, but obsoleted by the TCP Authentication Option (RFC 5925), which SHOULD be preferred when implemented.
  • IPsec, where there is not yet enough experience to give guidelines.
  • GTSM (RFC 5082): BGP speakers send TCP packets with TTL 255 instead of 1 and the receiver checks the value is 255. This stops spoofing from third parties that are not directly connected, and SHOULD be used on directly connected peerings. On multi-hop peerings it is less effective, because anyone inside the TTL diameter could spoof the TTL.

Session protection needs extra configuration to maintain, so it is NOT REQUIRED even at IXPs, but operators are RECOMMENDED to consider the trade-offs. Operators SHOULD also block spoofed packets with their own source addresses at all network edges (RFC 2827, RFC 3704), which protects internal BGP.
sections.plainLanguage: Put a guard on the door that only lets known neighbours knock. Use a secret handshake, and check that the knock came from right next door and not from far away.

sections.title: Prefix Filtering
sections.content:
The core of BGP security is controlling which prefixes are received and advertised. The RFC defines a set of reusable filters:

  • Special-purpose prefixes: use the IANA IPv4 and IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registries; prefixes marked "False" in the Global column SHOULD be discarded on Internet peerings.
  • Unallocated prefixes: IANA has allocated all the IPv4 space, so no filter is needed. For IPv6, filters can follow IANA allocations but must be kept current, within a maximum of one month of any change. If you cannot keep them updated, do not use them, because stale filters hurt the latest allocations.
  • Too specific: RIPE documented that IPv4 prefixes longer than /24 and IPv6 prefixes longer than /48 are generally neither announced nor accepted.
  • Own and downstream prefixes: a network SHOULD filter its own prefixes inbound, except where that breaks multihoming.
  • IXP LAN prefixes: SHOULD NOT accept more specifics from external peers, and only accept the prefix at all from ASes the IXP authorizes.
  • Default route: 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 are typically not accepted or advertised except in specific customer and provider setups.
sections.plainLanguage: Make a list of announcements you will ignore: ones that are impossible, too tiny, or that claim your own house belongs to someone else.

sections.title: Checking Who May Announce What
sections.content:
To confirm that an AS is entitled to announce a prefix, an operator can build filters from an Internet Routing Registry (IRR). A script takes the peer's AS number or AS-SET, recursively expands it to the AS numbers the peer is likely to announce, and fetches the prefixes registered for each. Filters built this way SHOULD be refreshed daily, since changes are sometimes made in an emergency. The approach can add tens of thousands of configuration lines for big peers, and operators SHOULD publish and maintain their own resources in the IRR.

The longer-term option is SIDR (RFC 6480). Origin validation (RFC 6811) checks the originating AS number, while path validation (BGPsec) was still ongoing work and could not yet be implemented. Operators SHOULD apply origin validation on top of existing practices, and SHOULD sign their own routing objects. Following RFC 7115, each external route is checked against the RPKI data.
sections.plainLanguage: Before believing someone who says a house is theirs, look it up in the official register. The register can be out of date, so check it often.

sections.title: Dampening, Maximum Prefixes and AS Paths
sections.content:
Route flap dampening penalises routes each time they change. Studies showed it could do more harm than good, and RIPE once recommended against it. After new thresholds were proposed (RFC 7196), this RFC RECOMMENDS using dampening with the adjusted thresholds.

Maximum prefixes: operators are RECOMMENDED to cap the routes accepted from a peer. From ordinary peers the limit should be lower than the number of routes in the Internet, so a peer suddenly sending the full table shuts the peering down. From an upstream providing full routing the limit should be higher than that number, to protect router memory. Limits should be reviewed regularly, and some vendors support a lower warning threshold that only logs.

AS path filtering rules include: accept from customers only paths with ASNs belonging to, or authorized to transit through, the customer; do not accept private AS numbers in the path unless the prefixes come from customers; do not accept a route whose first AS is not the peer's, unless the peer is a transparent route server; do not advertise prefixes with a nonempty AS path unless you provide transit for them; and do not accept your own AS number in the path.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not listen to a neighbour who keeps changing their mind every second. Stop listening if they suddenly shout a million directions. And throw out directions that pass through your own front door.

sections.title: Next Hops and Communities
sections.content:
On shared networks such as an IXP, BGP can advertise a third-party next hop, pointing traffic somewhere other than the announcing peer. Route servers do this on purpose. In direct peerings it is undesirable, since a peer could send traffic into a black hole or to an unsuspecting third party. An inbound policy SHOULD set the next hop to the sending peer's IXP address, but not on route-server peerings or where a third-party next hop is intentionally allowed.

The policy needs adjusting for Remote Triggered Black Holing (RFC 6666). A well-known next hop is statically routed to a null interface and, with a unicast RPF check, discards traffic to and from the prefix. Peers can signal this with an agreed BGP community.

For community scrubbing, operators SHOULD remove inbound communities carrying their own number in the high-order bits, allowing only those that customers and peers may use for signalling. They SHOULD NOT remove other communities, and SHOULD NOT generally remove the no-export community, since customers may need them to talk to upstreams.
sections.plainLanguage: When a neighbour says 'go ask my friend instead', be careful, because it might be a trap. Also, keep other people's sticky notes on the envelope unless they are fake ones using your name.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Scope Limits
sections.content:
The whole document is about BGP operational security: protecting the router and its sessions, using consistent prefix and AS path filters, and configuring other options to secure the BGP network.

It does not describe existing BGP implementations, their vulnerabilities, or how they handle errors, and it does not detail protection against attacks using crafted packets. Strict registry-based filtering carries its own warning: registries are not always accurate, so operators should check the impact first and make sure the solution is not worse than the problem.
sections.plainLanguage: This guide is about good habits for running BGP. It does not try to list every bug or every trick an attacker might use.
